title: Margin and Liquidation
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/0/body: With **isolated** margin, only the margin you assigned to that position is at risk. If you get liquidated, you lose **just that margin**, and the rest of your account balance stays untouched.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/1/body: With **cross** margin, your whole free futures balance backs your positions. Liquidation happens **later**, but when it does, it can take your **entire balance**.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/2/prompt: Your futures balance is 2,000 USDT. You opened a position with 200 USDT of isolated margin and got liquidated. Roughly how much did you lose?
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/2/explanati: With isolated margin, you only lose that position's margin (plus fees). The other 1,800 USDT stays safe.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/3/statement: Because cross margin delays liquidation, it's always less risky than isolated.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/3/explanati: Getting liquidated later means your loss can grow bigger. With cross, one bad position without a stop loss can take your whole account.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/4/body: Many traders recommend **isolated** margin to beginners, because each position's worst-case loss has a clear cap. Cross is more for people managing several positions at once. Either way, your **stop loss** is what really matters.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/4/tip: Isolated margin doesn't replace a stop loss; it only limits the worst case.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/5/pairs/0/m: Only that position's margin is at risk
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/5/pairs/1/m: Your whole balance backs your positions
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/6/sentence: With ___ margin, a liquidation can wipe out your ___.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/6/explanati: Cross uses your whole free balance to keep positions open, so its worst case is your whole balance too.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/7/prompt: In cross mode, you have one losing position and one winning position. If the first loss gets very large, what can happen?
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/7/options/0: Your balance and the other position's unrealized profit go to keeping the first one open
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/7/options/2: The exchange covers the loss itself
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/7/options/3: The two positions aren't connected at all
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/7/explanati: In cross, all positions draw from one shared balance. One position's loss can eat the others' unrealized profit and push them all toward liquidation.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/8/statement: With isolated margin, you can usually add margin after opening a position to push the liquidation price further away.
lessons/leverage-u2-l1/steps/8/explanati: Many exchanges let you do this. But if it's just to dodge liquidation on a bad trade, you're simply holding a loser with more money.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/0/body: When a position's loss grows so big that the remaining margin drops below a minimum called the **maintenance margin**, the exchange **force-closes** the position. This is called **liquidation**, and you usually lose almost all of that position's margin.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/1/body: With isolated margin and ignoring fees, your loss equals your whole margin when price moves about **1 ÷ leverage** against you. So a 10x long gets liquidated on a drop of **about 10%**; in practice **a little sooner**, because of maintenance margin.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/2/prompt: You went long Bitcoin from 60,000 at 10x with isolated margin. Roughly where is your liquidation price?
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/2/explanati: 1 ÷ 10 = 10%, and 10% below 60,000 is 54,000. Because of maintenance margin, the real liquidation happens a little above this number, so a little sooner.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/3/prompt: You went long from 60,000 at 10x with isolated margin, and the red line is your liquidation price. Tap the candle that liquidated your position.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/3/explanati: This candle's long wick touched your liquidation price, and that was enough to close the position. Price bouncing back above your entry afterward doesn't help you anymore; lower leverage or a proper stop loss would have kept you in the game.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/4/body: For a **short**, the liquidation price sits **above** your entry. A 20x short from 3,000 gets liquidated on a rise of about 5% (near 3,150). Your **stop loss** should always sit well **before** the liquidation price.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/4/tip: If your stop loss is past your liquidation price, you don't really have a stop loss.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/5/prompt: You shorted ETH from 3,000 at 25x with isolated margin. Roughly what percent does price need to rise to liquidate you?
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/5/explanati: 1 ÷ 25 = 4%, which is about 3,120. Maintenance margin makes liquidation come a little sooner, on a rise of slightly less than 4%.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/6/statement: Because of maintenance margin, liquidation usually happens a little before the exact "1 ÷ leverage" move.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/6/explanati: The exchange doesn't wait for your margin to hit exactly zero. Once it reaches the maintenance margin minimum, it closes the position.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/7/sentence: With leverage of ___, a long gets liquidated on about a 5% drop; at 50x, on about a ___ drop.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/7/explanati: 1 ÷ 20 = 5% and 1 ÷ 50 = 2%. The higher the leverage, the closer liquidation is.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/8/statement: If price returns to your entry after you get liquidated, your position reopens.
lessons/leverage-u2-l2/steps/8/explanati: Liquidation means the position was closed and its margin is gone. Whatever price does next has no effect on a position that no longer exists.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/0/body: The number you pick on the exchange (say, 20x) mostly decides **how much margin** you put up. Your account's real risk shows in your **effective leverage**: **total position value ÷ account balance**.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/1/body: Your whole account's loss depends on **effective leverage**: at 3x effective leverage, a 2% move against you means about a **6% loss on your whole account**, whether your set leverage is 5 or 50. Set leverage (in isolated mode) mostly changes your **distance to liquidation**.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/2/prompt: Your account holds 2,000 USDT. You have a BTC long worth 6,000 USDT and an ETH long worth 4,000 USDT open. What's your effective leverage?
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/2/explanati: (6,000 + 4,000) ÷ 2,000 = 5. Whatever each position's set leverage is, your whole account is exposed to the market 5 times over.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/3/prompt: With that same 5x effective leverage, if both markets move 3% against you, roughly what percent of your account do you lose?
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/4/body: Going long BTC, ETH and a few altcoins at the same time is really **one big bet on one direction**, because they usually move **together**. So calculate effective leverage for the **total of your same-direction positions**, not one by one.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/4/tip: Many careful traders keep their whole account's effective leverage low, say under 3x.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/5/statement: If you raise your set leverage from 10 to 50 but keep the position value the same, your dollar loss on each 1% price move gets 5 times bigger.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/5/explanati: Dollar loss = position value × price change. The position value didn't change, so the loss per 1% is the same; you just put up less margin and (in isolated mode) moved liquidation closer.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/6/pairs/0/m: Decides how much margin you need
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/6/pairs/3/m: Balance plus unrealized profit and loss
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/7/prompt: Ali and Sara each have 1,000 USDT, and both have stop losses 1% from entry. Ali opened a 1,000 USDT position at 50x, and Sara opened a 5,000 USDT position at 5x. Who's taking more risk?
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/7/options/0: Sara; her effective leverage is 5x and Ali's is 1x
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/7/options/3: You can't tell without knowing the direction
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/7/explanati: If the stops get hit, Ali loses 1,000 × 1% = 10 USDT and Sara loses 5,000 × 1% = 50 USDT. The leverage number on the exchange is misleading; what matters is position value relative to your account.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/8/sentence: Effective leverage = total value of your ___ divided by your account ___.
lessons/leverage-u2-l3/steps/8/explanati: Effective leverage shows how many times over your whole account is exposed to price moves, no matter what number you picked on the exchange.
